title: Does Seeing More Mean Knowing More? Mono-Anchored Advantage Normalization for Multi-Source Visual Reasoning
claim: Naive fusion of multiple sources yields confused, wrong outputs; anchoring on single-source signals filters noise and conflict to give accurate predictions.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right from input to outcome, orange highlight on ours
description: The figure reads left to right in three columns: Model Input, a reasoning method, and Reasoning Outcome. The left teal box holds the question "What's in the scene?" plus multi-source images (RGB, infrared, depth), each labeled with its own colored arrow. Two arrows lead to two stacked rows. The top gray row, "(a) Naive Reasoning", shows dashed arrows merging into a tangled-scribble node and a confused broken robot. It leads to a gray thought cloud with red uncertain text and an "Incorrect Prediction" red-cross badge. The bottom orange row, "(b) Mono-Anchored Reasoning (Ours)", shows a mono vs. multi balance-scale interaction and a happy robot. "Suppress Conflict" and "Filter Noise" arrows lead to an orange cloud with green correct text and an "Accurate Prediction" green-check badge. The orange panel draws the eye first.
caption: Illustration of multi-source visual reasoning. (a) Existing methods struggle to model dynamic interaction in multi-source data; (b) our method explicitly uses mono-source rewards as anchors to measure the information gain from multi-source integration and enhances reasoning.
abstract: Visual reasoning through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has achieved remarkable progress. However, when dealing with multi-source inputs, existing approaches tend to treat them as a mere accumulation of information, lacking explicit mechanisms to distinguish whether integrating additional sources yields information gain or introduces interference. Therefore, they struggle to effectively model dynamic interaction when integrating multiple sources, particularly when they differ significantly in physical properties and semantics, e.g., infrared and depth, leading to inferior performance to mono-source reasoning when a certain source holds the dominant signal. To address this issue, we propose MARS, a novel mono-anchored multi-source reasoning framework that models each visual modality as an independent information source. Specifically, by treating mono-source rewards as dynamic anchors, our method explicitly incorporates the information gain introduced by multi-source fusion into advantage normalization and adaptively emphasizes mutual promotion between sources while suppressing potential noise or conflicts during RLVR. From theoretical analysis, our method effectively quantifies information gain introduced by multi-source integration in gradient estimation, enabling consistent modality regulation. Empirical results also show impressive 3.2% and 4.9% performance gains on GRPO and DAPO across diverse datasets, confirming the effectiveness of our method. Code is available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/MARS.
